s: The Levites are joined to Aaron and his sons as a gift dedicated to the LORD to serve the Tent of Meeting, but they may not come near the vessels of the sanctuary or the altar on pain of death. They bear their own iniquity, receive all of Israel's tithe as their inheritance with no land, and must give a tithe of the tithe to Aaron the priest; they may eat the rest anywhere as their reward.

The children of Israel give the wave offerings, first fruits, devoted things, and firstborn, and their tithe goes to the Levites. They are forbidden to come near the Tent of Meeting lest they bear sin and die, and the LORD has taken the Levites from among them.
The Tent of Meeting is the place whose service the Levites perform and whose responsibility they keep. No stranger or ordinary Israelite may come near it, lest they bear sin and die.

The wave offerings of the children of Israel are given to Aaron, his sons, and his daughters as a portion forever, a covenant of salt, and may be eaten by everyone clean in the house. The Levites in turn must offer a wave offering of the tithe they receive, a tithe of the tithe, to the LORD by giving it to Aaron.

The holy things of the children of Israel, including the most holy offerings from the fire, are given to Aaron and his sons by reason of the anointing. The Levites are warned not to profane the holy things, lest they die.

The LORD gives all the tithe in Israel to the Levites as their inheritance in return for their service at the Tent of Meeting. The Levites must offer a tithe of it, its best part, as the LORD's wave offering to Aaron, after which the remainder is credited to them like threshing floor grain and wine press increase and may be eaten anywhere.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron and gives a statute for a red heifer without defect that has never been yoked. Eleazar the priest oversees its killing outside the camp, sprinkles its blood toward the Tent of Meeting seven times, and has it burned with cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet. A clean man gathers the ashes and stores them outside the camp for use in water for cleansing impurity, and those who handle the ritual become unclean until evening. The chapter then sets out the rules for touching a dead body, dying in a tent, or touching a bone or grave: seven days of uncleanness, with purification on the third and seventh days by water mixed with the ashes. Anyone who does not purify himself defiles the LORD's sanctuary and is cut off from Israel.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron and commands the statute of the red heifer. He declares that those who touch the dead and do not purify themselves defile his tabernacle and are cut off from Israel.

Eleazar receives the red heifer and brings it outside the camp, where it is killed before him. He sprinkles some of its blood with his finger toward the front of the Tent of Meeting seven times, and the burning takes place in his sight.

The children of Israel are told to bring a red heifer without spot or defect that was never yoked. The ashes are kept for their congregation, and the statute is to be perpetual for them and for the stranger living among them.

The red heifer must be without spot or defect and never yoked. It is killed outside the camp, its blood sprinkled seven times toward the Tent of Meeting, and its skin, meat, blood, and dung are burned, with cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet cast into the fire.

l: ashes of the heifer, Numbers, Chapter 19
s: A clean man gathers the ashes and lays them up in a clean place outside the camp, and they are called a sin offering. They are kept for use in water for cleansing impurity, and the one who gathers them is unclean until evening.

The water is made by putting ashes of the burnt sin offering into a vessel and pouring running water on them. A clean person sprinkles it with hyssop on the third and seventh days, and anyone who touches it is unclean until evening, as is the one who sprinkles it, who must wash his clothes.

Touching a dead person, or a slain person, a bone, or a grave in the open field, or being in a tent where a man dies, makes one unclean seven days. Open vessels without a bound covering are also unclean, and what the unclean person touches becomes unclean until evening.

The unclean person is sprinkled with the water for impurity on the third and seventh days, then washes his clothes and bathes in water and is clean at evening. Those who burn the heifer, gather the ashes, or sprinkle the water must also wash and are unclean until evening, and one who refuses purification is cut off for defiling the sanctuary.

The Israelites arrive in the wilderness of Zin and stay at Kadesh, where Miriam dies and is buried. With no water, the people quarrel with Moses and Aaron, and the LORD tells Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock so it pours out water. Moses instead rebukes the people and strikes the rock twice; water comes out, but the LORD tells Moses and Aaron they will not bring the assembly into the promised land because they did not believe him. Moses asks the king of Edom for passage along the king's highway, but Edom refuses and comes out against Israel with a strong hand, so Israel turns away. At Mount Hor the LORD announces Aaron's death, Moses transfers Aaron's garments to Eleazar, Aaron dies on the mountain, and the whole house of Israel mourns him thirty days.

Moses is blamed by the people for the lack of water, and he and Aaron fall on their faces at the Tent of Meeting. He takes the rod, calls the people rebels, and strikes the rock twice instead of speaking to it, and the LORD tells him he will not bring the assembly into the land. He also sends messengers to Edom requesting passage, and strips Aaron of his garments and puts them on Eleazar at Mount Hor.

Aaron joins Moses in facing the people's complaint and in gathering the assembly before the rock, and is told he will not enter the land because of the rebellion at the waters of Meribah. The LORD commands that he be taken up Mount Hor, where his garments are put on his son Eleazar and he dies on the mountain top. All the house of Israel weeps for him thirty days.

The LORD's glory appears to Moses and Aaron, and he instructs Moses to take the rod and speak to the rock to bring out water. He tells Moses and Aaron they did not believe him or sanctify him before Israel, so they will not bring the assembly into the land. He also announces and directs Aaron's death at Mount Hor.

The Israelites come to the wilderness of Zin and stay at Kadesh, where they quarrel with Moses and Aaron over lack of water and food, wishing they had died. They drink the water from the rock, are refused passage by Edom and turn away, and then come to Mount Hor, where they mourn Aaron for thirty days.

Edom's king receives Israel's message calling him brother and asking to pass along the king's highway. He refuses twice, threatening the sword, and comes out against Israel with many people and a strong hand, so Israel turns away.

Kadesh is where the Israelites stay in the wilderness of Zin, and where Miriam dies and is buried. Moses sends messengers from Kadesh to Edom, describing it as a city at the edge of Edom's border, and Israel later travels from there to Mount Hor.

Mount Hor is where the Israelites come after leaving Kadesh, by the border of the land of Edom. There the LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron, and Aaron dies on its top after his garments are given to Eleazar.

l: waters of Meribah of Kadesh, Numbers, Chapter 20
s: The waters of Meribah are named as the place where the children of Israel strove with the LORD and he was sanctified in them. The LORD later cites it as the place where Moses and Aaron rebelled against his word.
The LORD tells Moses to speak to the rock before the people's eyes so it will pour out water. Moses instead strikes it twice with his rod, and water comes out abundantly.

The lack of water for the congregation prompts the people's complaint against Moses and Aaron. Water comes out abundantly from the rock, and the congregation and their livestock drink. Israel also promises Edom to pay for any water they drink along the highway.

In Numbers 21, Israel vows to destroy the cities of the Canaanite king of Arad after he takes some of them captive, and the LORD delivers the Canaanites to them, so the place is named Hormah. While traveling around Edom, the people complain against God and Moses, and the LORD sends venomous snakes that kill many; when the people confess, Moses prays and makes a bronze serpent on a pole that heals those who look at it. Israel continues its journey through several camps to Beer, where the LORD provides water and the people sing a song to the well. Israel asks Sihon king of the Amorites for passage, he refuses and attacks, and Israel defeats him and settles in Heshbon and the Amorite cities. Israel then takes Jazer's villages and defeats Og king of Bashan at Edrei after the LORD tells Moses not to fear him.

Israel vows to destroy the Canaanite cities if the LORD delivers them, and the vow is fulfilled at Hormah. The people complain on the journey and are punished with snakes, then are healed through the bronze serpent, and they sing to the well at Beer. Israel defeats Sihon and Og, possesses their lands, and lives in the cities of the Amorites.

The LORD listens to Israel's vow and delivers the Canaanites into their hand. He sends venomous snakes against the complaining people, instructs Moses to make the serpent on a pole, and promises water at Beer. He also tells Moses not to fear Og and delivers Og into Israel's hand.

Moses is blamed by the people along with God, and prays for them when they confess their sin. He makes the bronze serpent on a pole at the LORD's command, sends to spy out Jazer, and is told by the LORD not to fear Og.
The LORD sends venomous snakes among the people as punishment for speaking against God and Moses. They bite the people, and many people of Israel die.

l: bronze serpent (Moses's bronze serpent), Numbers, Chapter 21
s: Moses makes a bronze serpent and sets it on a pole at the LORD's instruction. Anyone bitten by a serpent who looks at it lives.

The Amorites, under King Sihon, refuse Israel passage and fight them, and Israel strikes them down and takes their land from the Arnon to the Jabbok. Israel lives in their cities, and later drives out the Amorites at Jazer.

l: Sihon king of the Amorites, Numbers, Chapter 21
s: Sihon, king of the Amorites, refuses Israel passage through his border and gathers his people to fight them at Jahaz. Israel strikes him with the sword and takes his land. He is also recalled as having earlier taken the land of the former king of Moab up to the Arnon.

Heshbon is the city of Sihon king of the Amorites, and Israel lives in it and its villages after defeating him. A proverbial song says a fire went out from Heshbon and devoured Ar of Moab, and that Heshbon later perished as far as Dibon.

Og, king of Bashan, goes out with all his people to battle Israel at Edrei. The LORD tells Moses not to fear him, and Israel strikes him, his sons, and his people until none survive, and possesses his land.

Israel encamps in the plains of Moab, and Balak, king of Moab, fears them after seeing what they did to the Amorites. He sends elders of Moab and Midian with rewards of divination to summon Balaam the son of Beor to curse Israel. God first forbids Balaam to go and says Israel is blessed, but after a second, more honorable delegation God allows him to go if he speaks only God's word. On the way the LORD's angel blocks Balaam three times with a drawn sword, seen first only by Balaam's donkey, which the LORD enables to speak; Balaam then sees the angel, confesses sin, and is told to go on and speak only what he is given. Balak meets Balaam, offers sacrifices, and takes him up to the high places of Baal, where Balaam sees part of the people.

l: Balaam the son of Beor, Numbers, Chapter 22
s: Balaam is summoned by Balak to curse Israel and twice consults God, who first forbids him and then allows him to go with the princes of Moab if he speaks only God's word. He tells Balak's envoys he cannot go beyond the LORD's word even for a house full of silver and gold. On the road he strikes his donkey three times, is rebuked by the LORD's angel, confesses 'I have sinned,' and is told to speak only what he is given. He meets Balak, says he can speak only the word God puts in his mouth, and is brought to the high places of Baal, where he sees part of the people.

Balak, king of Moab, fears Israel and sends messengers, then a second and more honorable group of princes, to bring Balaam to curse them, promising great honor. He believes that whomever Balaam blesses is blessed and whomever he curses is cursed. He meets Balaam at the City of Moab, sacrifices cattle and sheep, and takes Balaam up to the high places of Baal to see part of Israel.

The children of Israel encamp in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho, having already defeated the Amorites. Moab fears them because they are many, likening them to an ox licking up grass. God tells Balaam that Israel is blessed and must not be cursed.

Moab is very afraid and distressed because of Israel's multitude, and its king Balak consults with the elders of Midian. Moab's elders and princes carry rewards of divination to Balaam and come back with a second delegation after he first refuses. Moab hopes to defeat Israel and drive them out of the land.

God asks Balaam who the men with him are and tells him not to go or curse Israel, 'for they are blessed.' Later he permits Balaam to go with the men, but only to do the word he speaks. His anger burns because Balaam went, and the LORD's angel is placed in the way against him.

l: angel of the LORD, Numbers, Chapter 22
s: The LORD's angel stands in Balaam's way as an adversary with a drawn sword, three times, in the path, in a narrow path between walls, and in a narrow place with no room to turn. After Balaam's eyes are opened, the angel rebukes him for striking the donkey, says Balaam's way is perverse, and says he would have killed Balaam and spared the donkey. He then tells Balaam to go with the men but speak only what he is told.

Balaam's donkey sees the angel and turns into the field, crushes Balaam's foot against a wall, and finally lies down under him, being struck each time. The LORD opens her mouth and she asks what she has done to deserve three blows, reminding Balaam she has carried him all his life. The angel says her turning away saved Balaam's life and that he would have spared her.

Balak seeks a curse on Israel through Balaam so that Moab may strike them and drive them out. God forbids it, declaring Israel blessed, and Balaam repeatedly affirms he can speak only the word God gives. By the end of the unit Balaam has been brought to the high places of Baal and sees part of the people, but no curse has yet been spoken.

Balaam instructs Balak to build seven altars and offer a bull and a ram on each, then goes to a bare height where God meets him and puts a word in his mouth. Returning to Balak and the princes of Moab, Balaam declares he cannot curse whom God has not cursed, and instead praises Israel as a numerous people dwelling alone. Balak protests, then takes Balaam to the top of Pisgah in the field of Zophim, where the altars and offerings are repeated and Balaam again speaks the LORD's word: God does not lie or repent, has commanded a blessing, and sees no iniquity in Jacob. Balak tells him neither to curse nor bless, but Balaam insists he must do all the LORD speaks. Balak then takes him to the top of Peor, where Balaam again asks for seven altars, seven bulls and seven rams, and Balak complies.

l: Balaam the son of Beor, Numbers, Chapter 23
s: Balaam directs the building of altars and offerings at three sites, meets God, and speaks only the word the LORD puts in his mouth. He refuses to curse Israel, pronouncing instead that God has not cursed or defied them and that he cannot reverse the blessing. He wishes to die the death of the righteous and tells Balak that he must do all the LORD speaks.

Balak, king of Moab, asks Balaam to curse Jacob and Israel, and builds the altars and offers the sacrifices Balaam requests. When Balaam blesses instead, Balak objects and moves him to Pisgah and then to Peor, hoping a different place will let him curse them. At last he tells Balaam to neither curse nor bless them.

The LORD meets Balaam, puts a word in his mouth, and sends him back to Balak to speak it. Balaam says God has not cursed or defied Israel, is not a man who lies or repents, has commanded a blessing, and is with Israel, having brought them out of Egypt.

Israel, also called Jacob, is described as a people dwelling alone and not listed among the nations, too numerous to count. It is said that the LORD sees no iniquity or perverseness in it, that God brought it out of Egypt with the strength of a wild ox, and that it rises like a lioness and a lion that will not lie down until it eats the prey.
Seven altars are built at Balaam's request at the first place, again at Pisgah, and a third set at Peor. On each altar a bull and a ram are offered, as a setting for Balaam to meet God.

l: burnt offerings (bulls and rams), Numbers, Chapter 23
s: A bull and a ram are offered on each of the seven altars at each of the places. Balak stands by his burnt offering with the princes of Moab while Balaam goes off to meet God. At Peor, Balaam again requests seven bulls and seven rams, and Balak offers them.

Balak asks Balaam to curse and defy Jacob and Israel, and tries from different places where Balaam may see only part of them. Balaam says he cannot curse whom God has not cursed, and that there is no enchantment or divination against Israel. Balak finally tells him neither to curse nor bless them.

Balaam blesses Israel instead of cursing, which Balak calls blessing them altogether. He says he has received a command to bless, that God has blessed and he cannot reverse it, and that it will be said of Jacob and Israel, 'What has God done!'

Balaam, seeing that the LORD is pleased to bless Israel, stops using divination and looks toward the wilderness, where he sees Israel camped by tribes and is seized by the Spirit of God. He delivers a parable praising Israel's tents, its strength, its king, and its safety, declaring that those who bless Israel are blessed and those who curse it are cursed. Balak angrily strikes his hands together, rebukes Balaam for blessing his enemies three times, and tells him to flee, while Balaam answers that he can only say what the LORD says. Balaam then gives further parables foretelling a star and scepter from Jacob and Israel that will crush Moab, Edom, and Seir, and pronounces destruction on Amalek, the Kenite, Asshur, and Eber. Balaam and Balak then each go their own way.

l: Balaam the son of Beor, Numbers, Chapter 24
s: Balaam, seeing that the LORD is pleased to bless Israel, abandons divination and turns toward the wilderness, where the Spirit of God comes on him. He speaks two parables blessing Israel and foretelling its future, plus short oracles on Amalek, the Kenite, and others. He tells Balak that he cannot go beyond the LORD's word even for a house full of silver and gold, then returns to his place.

Balak is angry that Balaam has blessed rather than cursed his enemies three times, and he strikes his hands together. He tells Balaam to flee, saying he had meant to promote him to great honor but the LORD has kept him back from it. After Balaam's final oracles, Balak goes his own way.

Israel is seen dwelling according to its tribes, and its tents and dwellings are called goodly. It is described as well watered, brought out of Egypt by God, and as strong as a wild ox, and likened to a lion that no one can rouse. Balaam foretells that a star and scepter from Jacob will crush Moab and the sons of Sheth, make Edom and Seir possessions, and that everyone who blesses Israel is blessed and everyone who curses it is cursed.

The LORD is pleased to bless Israel, and his word is what Balaam says he cannot go beyond. The Spirit of God comes on Balaam, and God is said to bring Israel out of Egypt. Balak says the LORD has kept Balaam back from honor.

Balaam delivers two main parables, each opened with the formula that the man whose eyes are open speaks. The first blesses Israel's tents, prosperity, king, and strength, while the second looks to the latter days, with a star and scepter from Jacob conquering Moab, Edom, and Seir. Three shorter parables follow, announcing destruction for Amalek, the Kenite, and Asshur and Eber, the last of which says ships from Kittim will afflict them.

While Israel stayed in Shittim, the people took part in sacrifices to the gods of the daughters of Moab and joined themselves to Baal Peor, provoking the LORD's anger. The LORD told Moses to hang the chiefs, and Moses told the judges to kill those who had joined Baal Peor. When Zimri, a Simeonite prince, brought the Midianite woman Cozbi before Moses and the congregation, Phinehas, son of Eleazar, speared them both, which stopped the plague that had killed twenty-four thousand. The LORD then gave Phinehas a covenant of peace and an everlasting priesthood for his offspring because he was jealous for his God and made atonement. The LORD also commanded Moses to harass and strike the Midianites for deceiving Israel in the matter of Peor and Cozbi.

Israel stayed in Shittim, where the people ate and bowed down at sacrifices to the gods of the daughters of Moab and joined themselves to Baal Peor. This brought the LORD's anger and a plague that killed twenty-four thousand, which stopped after Phinehas acted. Israel was spared from being consumed through Phinehas's jealousy.

Baal Peor is the god to whom Israel joined itself at Shittim, which kindled the LORD's anger. Moses ordered that those who had joined themselves to Baal Peor be killed, and the Midianites are later blamed for deceiving Israel in the matter of Peor.

The LORD's anger burned against Israel for joining Baal Peor, and he ordered the chiefs hanged before the sun to turn away his anger. He praised Phinehas for turning away his wrath, gave him a covenant of peace and an everlasting priesthood, and commanded Moses to harass and strike the Midianites.

Moses received the LORD's command to hang the chiefs of the people and told Israel's judges to kill each man who had joined himself to Baal Peor. He and the congregation were weeping at the door of the Tent of Meeting when Zimri brought Cozbi in. He was then told to relay the covenant to Phinehas and to harass the Midianites.

Phinehas, son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron the priest, rose from the congregation, took a spear, and thrust through Zimri and Cozbi in the pavilion, stopping the plague. The LORD said he was jealous with his jealousy and made atonement for Israel, and gave him a covenant of peace and an everlasting priesthood for him and his offspring.

Zimri, son of Salu and a prince of a fathers' house among the Simeonites, was the man of Israel who brought a Midianite woman to his brothers in sight of Moses and the congregation. Phinehas killed him along with the woman.

Cozbi, daughter of Zur, who was head of the people of a fathers' house in Midian, was the Midianite woman brought by Zimri. Phinehas thrust her through the body, and she was slain on the day of the plague. The LORD cites the incident regarding her as grounds for striking the Midianites.

The LORD commanded Moses to harass and strike the Midianites because they harassed Israel with wiles and deceived them in the matter of Peor and in the incident regarding Cozbi, daughter of the prince of Midian. The Midianite woman Cozbi was slain with Zimri.
The plague struck Israel as a result of the people's joining Baal Peor and was stopped when Phinehas speared Zimri and Cozbi. Twenty-four thousand died by it.

After the plague, the LORD tells Moses and Eleazar the priest to take a census of Israelite men twenty years old and upward who can go to war, on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho. The chapter lists each tribe's families and counts, including Reuben, Simeon, Gad, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Manasseh, Ephraim, Benjamin, Dan, Asher, and Naphtali, for a total of 601,730. The LORD directs that the land be divided by lot among the tribes, with larger tribes receiving more inheritance and smaller ones less. The Levites are counted separately, 23,000 males from a month old and upward, because they receive no inheritance among the Israelites. The chapter ends by noting that none of those counted earlier at Sinai remained, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun, because the LORD had said they would die in the wilderness.

The LORD commands Moses and Eleazar to take a census of Israelite men twenty and older able to go to war. He instructs that the land be divided by lot as an inheritance, with more given to the larger tribes and less to the smaller. The text recalls that He had said the earlier generation would surely die in the wilderness, sparing only Caleb and Joshua.

Moses is commanded by the LORD, together with Eleazar the priest, to take the census, and he speaks with the people on the plains of Moab. He is named as a son of Amram and Jochebed, brother of Aaron and Miriam. He receives the LORD's instructions for dividing the land by lot.

Eleazar the priest is addressed by the LORD along with Moses and conducts the census with him on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho. He is listed as one of Aaron's sons, with Nadab, Abihu, and Ithamar. Nadab and Abihu are noted as having died when they offered strange fire before the LORD.

The children of Israel are counted by tribe and family, with a total of 601,730 men twenty and older able to go to war. The text says none of those counted earlier at Sinai remained, except Caleb and Joshua. The tribes are to inherit the land by lot according to their numbers.

The LORD orders a census of all Israelite men twenty years old and upward who can go to war, carried out by Moses and Eleazar on the plains of Moab. It records each tribe's families and totals, giving 601,730 overall. Its purpose is tied to dividing the land, and it contains none of the men counted earlier at Sinai except Caleb and Joshua.

l: land inheritance by lot, Numbers, Chapter 26
s: The LORD says the land is to be divided as an inheritance according to the number of names, giving more to the larger tribes and less to the smaller. It is also to be divided by lot, and the tribes inherit according to their fathers' tribal names. The Levites receive no inheritance among the Israelites.

The Levites are counted separately by family: Gershonites, Kohathites, and Merarites, along with the Libnites, Hebronites, Mahlites, Mushites, and Korahites. They number 23,000, every male from a month old and upward. They are not counted among the children of Israel because no inheritance is given them among them.

The five daughters of Zelophehad (Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah) come before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the princes and the congregation to ask for a possession among their father's brothers, since he died without sons. Moses brings the case to the LORD, who affirms they speak rightly and gives a statute for the inheritance of those who die without sons, passing it to daughters, then brothers, then father's brothers, then the nearest kinsman. The LORD then tells Moses to go up Mount Abarim to see the land, and that he will be gathered to his people as Aaron was, because he rebelled at the waters of Meribah of Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin. Moses asks the LORD to appoint a man over the congregation so it will not be like sheep without a shepherd. The LORD names Joshua the son of Nun, and Moses commissions him before Eleazar and the congregation by laying his hands on him.

The daughters of Zelophehad, named Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah, came before Moses, Eleazar, the princes and the congregation at the door of the Tent of Meeting. They argued that their father's name should not be lost for lack of a son and asked for a possession among their father's brothers, and the LORD declared that they speak right.

Zelophehad, son of Hepher, of the families of Manasseh, died in the wilderness in his own sin and had no sons. He was not part of Korah's company that gathered against the LORD, and his daughters were granted his inheritance.

Moses brought the daughters' case before the LORD and was told to give them an inheritance and to announce the statute to Israel. He was also told to go up Mount Abarim, see the land, and then be gathered to his people because of his rebellion at Meribah. He asked the LORD to appoint a successor and commissioned Joshua as commanded.

Eleazar the priest was present when the daughters of Zelophehad made their request. He was designated to stand with Joshua, inquiring for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD, and Joshua was set before him at his commissioning.

The congregation witnessed the daughters' plea at the Tent of Meeting. Moses prayed that it not be like sheep without a shepherd, and it was told to obey Joshua, who would lead its going out and coming in.

The LORD affirmed that the daughters of Zelophehad speak right and established the inheritance statute for Israel. He told Moses he would die after seeing the land because of his rebellion at Meribah, and he chose Joshua, a man in whom is the Spirit, to lead the congregation.

l: inheritance law for daughters, Numbers, Chapter 27
s: The LORD established that if a man dies with no son, his inheritance passes to his daughter. If he has no daughter it goes to his brothers, then to his father's brothers, and then to his nearest kinsman, and this was made a statute and ordinance for Israel.

Joshua the son of Nun was named by the LORD as a man in whom is the Spirit and was chosen to lead the congregation after Moses. He was set before Eleazar and the congregation, received Moses' laying on of hands, and was given authority to be obeyed.

At the LORD's command, Moses took Joshua, set him before Eleazar the priest and the whole congregation, laid his hands on him, and commissioned him in their sight. This gave Joshua authority so that the congregation would obey him, with Eleazar to inquire for him by the Urim.

In Numbers 28 the LORD speaks to Moses and commands him to instruct the children of Israel to present the LORD's offerings made by fire in their due season. The chapter sets out the continual daily burnt offering of two year-old male lambs, one in the morning and one at evening, with fine flour, oil and a drink offering. It then specifies larger offerings for the Sabbath and for the beginning of each month, the latter including bulls, a ram, lambs and a male goat as a sin offering. Finally it lays out the offerings for the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month, the seven-day feast of unleavened bread starting on the fifteenth, and the day of the first fruits at the feast of weeks, each with holy convocations, no regular work on the key days, and offerings that are in addition to the continual burnt offering.

The LORD speaks to Moses and commands that the children of Israel present his offerings, his food made by fire, as a pleasant aroma in their due season. He specifies the animals, flour, oil and drink offerings for the daily, Sabbath, monthly and festival offerings, and he is the one to whom Passover belongs, as the LORD's Passover.

The children of Israel are to be commanded, through Moses, to present the LORD's offerings in their due season. They are to offer the continual, Sabbath, monthly and festival offerings, keep holy convocations, and do no regular work on the first and seventh days of unleavened bread and on the day of first fruits.

The continual burnt offering consists of two male lambs a year old without defect, offered day by day, with fine flour mixed with beaten oil and a drink offering. It was ordained at Mount Sinai as a pleasant aroma to the LORD, and all the Sabbath, monthly and festival offerings are made in addition to it.

l: morning and evening lambs (continual burnt offering), Numbers, Chapter 28
s: One male lamb a year old without defect is offered in the morning and the other at evening. Each is accompanied by one tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a fourth of a hin of beaten oil, and a drink offering of a fourth of a hin of strong drink, poured out in the holy place.

The meal offering is fine flour mixed with oil, offered with the burnt offerings. The amounts are one tenth of an ephah per lamb, two tenths for a ram, and three tenths for a bull, with two tenths for the Sabbath's two lambs; the daily one is mixed with a fourth of a hin of beaten oil.

The drink offering accompanies the burnt offerings: a fourth of a hin of strong drink for each daily lamb, poured in the holy place. For the monthly offering it is half a hin of wine for a bull, a third of a hin for the ram, and a fourth of a hin for a lamb.

On the Sabbath day two male lambs a year old without defect are offered, with two tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil as a meal offering, and the drink offering. This is the burnt offering of every Sabbath, in addition to the continual burnt offering and its drink offering.

At the beginning of each month a burnt offering is made of two young bulls, one ram and seven male lambs a year old without defect, with meal offerings of fine flour mixed with oil and the prescribed drink offerings. One male goat is also offered as a sin offering, in addition to the continual burnt offering and its drink offering.
The LORD's Passover falls on the fourteenth day of the first month. The feast of unleavened bread follows on the fifteenth day.

l: Feast of Unleavened Bread, Numbers, Chapter 28
s: Beginning on the fifteenth day of the first month, unleavened bread is eaten for seven days, with a holy convocation and no regular work on the first and seventh days. Each day two young bulls, one ram and seven male lambs are offered with their meal offerings, plus one male goat as a sin offering to make atonement, in addition to the continual burnt offering.

On the day of the first fruits, when a new meal offering is brought to the LORD at the feast of weeks, there is a holy convocation and no regular work. The offering is two young bulls, one ram and seven male lambs with their meal offerings, and one male goat to make atonement, besides the continual burnt offering, its meal offering and drink offerings, all without defect.

Chapter 29 sets out the offerings the LORD commands for the holy days of the seventh month. On the first day there is a holy convocation and a day of blowing of trumpets, with a burnt offering of one bull, one ram and seven lambs plus a goat for a sin offering. On the tenth day the people are to afflict their souls and do no work, offering the same animals and a sin offering in addition to the sin offering of atonement. From the fifteenth day a seven-day feast is kept, with bulls decreasing daily from thirteen to seven, and a solemn assembly on the eighth day. The chapter ends with Moses telling the children of Israel all that the LORD commanded him.

The LORD commands the offerings for the seventh-month holy days, specifying the animals, meal offerings and drink offerings. These are described as a pleasant aroma and offerings made by fire to Him. All of this is what He commanded Moses.
Moses relays the LORD's instructions about the seventh-month feasts and offerings. He tells the children of Israel according to all that the LORD commanded him.

The children of Israel are instructed to hold holy convocations, refrain from regular work, and bring the prescribed offerings on the first, tenth, fifteenth and eighth-after-fifteenth days of the seventh month. They are told to offer these in their set feasts in addition to their vows and free will offerings. Moses tells them all that the LORD commanded.

Held on the first day of the seventh month, it is a holy convocation with no regular work, described as a day of blowing of trumpets. It requires a burnt offering of one young bull, one ram and seven male lambs with meal offerings, plus one male goat for a sin offering, in addition to the new moon and continual offerings.

On the tenth day of the seventh month there is a holy convocation on which the people are to afflict their souls and do no kind of work. The offerings are one young bull, one ram, seven male lambs and a male goat for a sin offering, in addition to the sin offering of atonement and the continual burnt offering.

Beginning on the fifteenth day of the seventh month with a holy convocation and no regular work, this is a feast to the LORD lasting seven days. Each day requires two rams, fourteen lambs and a goat for a sin offering, with bulls decreasing from thirteen on the first day to seven on the seventh.

The eighth day is a solemn assembly with no regular work. The offering is reduced to one bull, one ram, seven male lambs and one male goat for a sin offering, with meal and drink offerings according to their number.

Burnt offerings of bulls, rams and male lambs a year old without defect are prescribed for each holy day as a pleasant aroma to the LORD. They are accompanied by meal offerings of fine flour mixed with oil and by drink offerings, and are in addition to the continual burnt offering.

One male goat is required as a sin offering on each of the holy days, beginning with the first day, where it is to make atonement for the people. It is always given in addition to the continual burnt offering, and on the tenth day also in addition to the sin offering of atonement.

Moses addresses the heads of the tribes of Israel with the LORD's command about vows. A man who vows or swears an oath to the LORD must not break his word and must do all that comes out of his mouth. A young woman in her father's house, or a married woman, has her vows stand if her father or husband hears them and says nothing, but they are void if he forbids her on the day he hears. The vows of a widow or divorced woman stand against her, and a husband who nullifies a vow after the day he heard it bears her iniquity.

Moses speaks to the heads of the tribes of the children of Israel and relays what the LORD has commanded about vows. The chapter closes by calling these the statutes the LORD commanded Moses concerning husband and wife, and father and daughter.
The LORD is the one who commands the statutes on vows and to whom vows and oaths are made. He is said to forgive a woman whose vow is forbidden by her father or made void by her husband.

l: woman (young, in her father's house), Numbers, Chapter 30
s: A young woman living in her father's house who vows a vow or binds herself by a pledge has her vows stand if her father hears and says nothing. If her father forbids her on the day he hears, none of her vows stand and the LORD will forgive her.
The father hears his young daughter's vows and pledges. If he says nothing, they stand; if he forbids her on the day he hears, they do not stand.

The husband may establish or make void his wife's vows and binding oaths. If he says nothing on the day he hears them, they stand, and if he forbids them that day they are void. If he nullifies them after he has heard them, he bears her iniquity.

Vows and binding oaths to the LORD must not be broken by a man, who must do all that proceeds out of his mouth. A woman's vows stand or fall depending on whether her father or husband says nothing or forbids them on the day he hears, while those of a widow or divorced woman stand against her.

The LORD commands Moses to avenge Israel on the Midianites, and Moses sends twelve thousand men, a thousand from each tribe, with Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest. They kill every male, including five Midianite kings and Balaam son of Beor, burn the cities and encampments, and bring captives and plunder back to the camp. Moses is angry that the women were kept alive and orders the killing of every male child and every woman who has known a man, while the girls who have not known a man are kept alive. Moses and Eleazar set out purification rules for the soldiers, captives, and goods, and the LORD directs how the plunder is divided between the soldiers and the congregation, with tribute set aside for Eleazar and the Levites. The officers report that not one man is missing and bring a gold offering of 16,750 shekels, which Moses and Eleazar place in the Tent of Meeting as a memorial.

The LORD commands Moses to avenge Israel on Midian and later directs how the plunder is counted and divided, including the tribute due to him. The text states that the war was fought as he commanded, and he receives a wave offering and the officers' gold.

Moses relays the LORD's command, has a thousand men from each tribe armed, and sends them to war. He is angry with the officers for keeping the women alive and orders the killing of all male little ones and all women who have known a man. He also directs the purification, divides the plunder, gives the tribute to Eleazar and the Levites, and receives the officers' gold.

Eleazar, with Moses and the princes, meets the returning army outside the camp and tells the soldiers the statute for purifying metals and other goods. He receives the LORD's wave offering of the soldiers' half of the plunder and, with Moses, takes the officers' gold into the Tent of Meeting.

The Midianites are attacked by Israel, and every male is killed, including their five kings, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba. Their cities and encampments are burned, and their women, children, livestock, and goods are taken. Moses says their women caused Israel to trespass at Peor through Balaam's counsel.

The children of Israel are to be avenged on Midian, and each tribe supplies a thousand men for the war. They take the plunder and divide it into two halves, with the congregation's half taxed one in fifty for the Levites.

l: army of Israel (twelve thousand men of war), Numbers, Chapter 31
s: Twelve thousand men, a thousand from each tribe, fight Midian and kill every male, the five kings, and Balaam. They burn Midian's cities and bring back captives and plunder. They must camp outside for seven days and purify themselves, and their half of the plunder is taxed one in five hundred for the LORD. Their officers report that not one man is lacking.

l: officers (captains of thousands and hundreds), Numbers, Chapter 31
s: Moses is angry with the captains of thousands and hundreds for saving the women alive. Afterward they report that none of their men is missing and bring a gold offering to make atonement for their souls.

The women of Midian are taken captive with their little ones. Moses blames them for the matter of Peor through Balaam's counsel and orders every woman who has known a man killed, while the girls who have not are kept alive. Thirty-two thousand such girls are counted among the plunder.

The plunder includes 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys, and 32,000 persons, and it is divided into two equal halves. From the soldiers' half one in five hundred goes to Eleazar as the LORD's offering, and from the congregation's half one in fifty goes to the Levites. The men of war also took booty for themselves.

l: gold offering of the officers, Numbers, Chapter 31
s: The captains of thousands and hundreds bring gold ornaments, armlets, bracelets, signet rings, earrings, and necklaces as an offering to make atonement for their souls. It totals 16,750 shekels, and Moses and Eleazar bring it into the Tent of Meeting as a memorial for Israel before the LORD.

The war is commanded by the LORD as vengeance on Midian and is fought by twelve thousand men with Phinehas, carrying the sanctuary vessels and trumpets. The Israelites kill every male, burn the cities, and return with captives and plunder, and no Israelite is reported lost.

Anyone who killed or touched the slain must camp outside for seven days and purify themselves on the third and seventh days, along with their captives. Garments and items of skin, goats' hair, and wood are purified, and metals that withstand fire go through the fire and the water for impurity, while other things go through water. The men wash their clothes on the seventh day before entering the camp.

The children of Reuben and the children of Gad, who own very great multitudes of livestock, ask Moses, Eleazar the priest, and the princes to give them the land east of the Jordan, including Jazer and Gilead, and not bring them over the Jordan. Moses rebukes them, comparing them to their fathers who discouraged Israel at Kadesh Barnea and caused the LORD to make the people wander forty years. The two tribes promise to build folds and cities for their families and livestock but to go armed before the children of Israel until all have received their inheritance. Moses accepts on condition that they cross the Jordan armed and help subdue the land, otherwise they will receive possessions in Canaan, and he gives them, along with the half-tribe of Manasseh, the kingdoms of Sihon and Og. The tribes rebuild and rename cities, and Machir, Jair, and Nobah take Gilead and its villages.

The children of Reuben, with Gad, ask for the land east of the Jordan because of their livestock, and promise to cross the Jordan armed ahead of Israel. They are granted the land on that condition and build Heshbon, Elealeh, Kiriathaim, Nebo, Baal Meon, and Sibmah, giving some cities new names.

The children of Gad, with Reuben, request the livestock land east of the Jordan and agree to fight armed before Israel until all have their inheritance. They receive the land with Reuben and build Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer, Atroth-shophan, Jazer, Jogbehah, Beth Nimrah, and Beth Haran as fortified cities and sheepfolds.

Moses rebukes Reuben and Gad, recalling how the earlier generation discouraged Israel and was made to wander forty years. He then sets the condition that they cross the Jordan armed to subdue the land, warns that their sin will find them out otherwise, and instructs Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of households accordingly. He gives the tribes of Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh the kingdoms of Sihon and Og, and gives Gilead to Machir.

The LORD is recalled as having struck the land east of the Jordan before Israel and as having sworn in anger that the generation from Egypt aged twenty and up, except Caleb and Joshua, would not see the promised land. His anger led to forty years of wandering. Moses frames the war and the Reubenite and Gadite obligation as being 'before the LORD.'

The children of Israel are the people whose hearts Moses fears Reuben and Gad will discourage from entering the land the LORD gave them. Reuben and Gad promise to go armed before them and not return home until every Israelite has received an inheritance.

Gilead is seen by Reuben and Gad as a place suited to livestock, and the two tribes plan to leave their families, flocks, and cities there. Moses conditionally grants it to them, and Machir son of Manasseh takes it, dispossesses the Amorites, and is given Gilead by Moses to live in.

The Jordan is the boundary between the eastern land Reuben and Gad want and the land of Canaan. The two tribes ask not to be brought over it, but then agree that their armed men will cross it before the LORD and keep their inheritance on the east side.

Canaan is the land across the Jordan that Israel is to enter and subdue. Moses says that if Reuben and Gad do not cross armed, they will have possessions among the others in Canaan, and the two tribes promise to cross armed into it.

l: livestock (of Reuben and Gad), Numbers, Chapter 32
s: The very great multitudes of livestock owned by Reuben and Gad are the stated reason for their request, since the land of Jazer and Gilead suits livestock. The tribes plan to build sheepfolds for them, and their livestock stay in the cities of Gilead while the men go to war.

l: Reubenite and Gadite land request, Numbers, Chapter 32
s: Reuben and Gad ask Moses, Eleazar, and the princes for the eastern land as a possession and not to be brought over the Jordan. After Moses's rebuke, the request is accepted on the condition that their armed men fight alongside Israel until the land is subdued, and the tribes agree. The land is then given to them, along with half of Manasseh.

The coming conquest of Canaan is the war in which Reuben and Gad pledge to take part, crossing the Jordan armed before the LORD until enemies are driven out and the land subdued. Moses's rebuke refers to the earlier failure at Kadesh Barnea, when discouragement kept the earlier generation from entering. After the conquest, the two tribes would be free of obligation and return to their eastern land.

Numbers 33 records the stages of the children of Israel's journey from Rameses in Egypt to the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, which Moses wrote down at the LORD's command. It recalls that they left on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after the Passover, while the Egyptians buried their firstborn and the LORD executed judgments on Egyptian gods. The list names encampments including Succoth, Marah, Elim, Rephidim, the wilderness of Sinai, Kadesh, and Mount Hor, where Aaron died at age 123 in the fortieth year. At the plains of Moab the LORD tells Moses to instruct Israel that, once across the Jordan into Canaan, they must drive out the inhabitants, destroy their idols and high places, and divide the land by lot. He warns that any inhabitants left in place will become pricks in their eyes and thorns in their sides, and that he will do to Israel what he planned to do to them.

The children of Israel left Egypt by their armies under Moses and Aaron and traveled through many encampments to the plains of Moab. There they camped by the Jordan from Beth Jeshimoth to Abel Shittim and were commanded to drive out Canaan's inhabitants and inherit the land by lot.

Moses led Israel with Aaron and wrote down the starting points of their journeys at the LORD's command. In the plains of Moab the LORD spoke to him and told him to relay instructions about entering Canaan.
Aaron, with Moses, led Israel out of Egypt. He went up Mount Hor at the LORD's command and died there on the first day of the fifth month in the fortieth year after the exodus, at age 123.

The LORD commanded Moses to record the journeys, had struck the Egyptian firstborn and executed judgments on Egypt's gods. At the plains of Moab he commanded Israel to dispossess Canaan's inhabitants, said he had given them the land, and warned he would do to Israel what he planned for the inhabitants if they failed.
Canaan is the land Israel will enter by crossing the Jordan, and the LORD says he has given it to them to possess. Its king of Arad, who lived in the South, heard of Israel's coming.

The plains of Moab, by the Jordan at Jericho, are the final encampment of the journey list, stretching from Beth Jeshimoth to Abel Shittim. There the LORD spoke to Moses about taking possession of Canaan.

The journeys are listed as a series of departures and encampments from Rameses through Succoth, Marah, Elim, Sinai, Kadesh, Mount Hor, and Abarim to the plains of Moab. Moses wrote down the starting points by the LORD's commandment.

Israel went out of Egypt from Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after the Passover, with a high hand in sight of all the Egyptians. This happened as the Egyptians buried their firstborn, whom the LORD had struck, and as he executed judgments on their gods.

The inhabitants of Canaan are to be driven out before Israel, and their stone idols, molten images, and high places destroyed. If any are left, they will be like pricks in Israel's eyes and thorns in its sides and will harass Israel.

l: land inheritance by lot, Numbers, Chapter 33
s: The LORD commands that Israel inherit the land by lot according to families and the tribes of their fathers. Larger groups receive a larger inheritance and smaller groups a smaller one, and wherever the lot falls to a man, that is his.

The LORD speaks to Moses and gives him the boundaries of the land of Canaan, which will fall to the children of Israel as an inheritance. The south, west, north, and east borders are described through a series of named landmarks, including the Salt Sea, the great sea, Mount Hor, Hazar Enan, and the Jordan. Moses relays to the people that the land is to be inherited by lot by the nine tribes and the half-tribe, since Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh have already received their inheritance east of the Jordan. The LORD then names Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun to divide the land, together with one prince from each of the nine and a half tribes, and the chapter lists those princes by name.

The LORD speaks to Moses twice, first giving the borders of the land of Canaan and then naming the men who will divide it. He commands that the land be given as an inheritance to the nine tribes and the half-tribe.

Moses receives the LORD's instructions about the borders and about the men who will divide the land. He commands the children of Israel, telling them that the land is to be inherited by lot and that two and a half tribes have already received their inheritance east of the Jordan.
The children of Israel are commanded, through Moses, about the land they will enter and inherit. They are told its borders and that it will be allotted by lot to the nine tribes and the half-tribe.

The land of Canaan is described as the land that will fall to Israel as an inheritance, and its borders are set out on all four sides. It is the land the LORD has commanded to be given to the nine tribes and the half-tribe.
Eleazar the priest is named by the LORD as one of the men who shall divide the land for inheritance. He is listed together with Joshua the son of Nun.
Joshua the son of Nun is named by the LORD, along with Eleazar the priest, as one of those who shall divide the land for inheritance.

l: nine tribes and the half-tribe, Numbers, Chapter 34
s: The nine tribes and the half-tribe are the ones to whom the LORD commands that the land of Canaan be given by lot. Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh have already received their inheritance beyond the Jordan at Jericho eastward, toward the sunrise.

l: borders of the land, Numbers, Chapter 34
s: The south border runs from the wilderness of Zin by Edom and the end of the Salt Sea, past the ascent of Akrabbim, Kadesh Barnea, Hazar Addar, and Azmon to the brook of Egypt and the sea. The west border is the great sea, the north border runs from the great sea to Mount Hor, the entrance of Hamath, Zedad, Ziphron, and Hazar Enan, and the east border runs from Hazar Enan through Shepham, Riblah, and the sea of Chinnereth, down the Jordan to the Salt Sea.

l: division of the land by lot, Numbers, Chapter 34
s: Moses tells the people that the land is to be inherited by lot, as the LORD commanded, for the nine tribes and the half-tribe. The LORD names Eleazar, Joshua, and one prince from each tribe as the men who will carry out the division.

l: princes of the tribes, Numbers, Chapter 34
s: The LORD instructs that one prince from each tribe be taken to help divide the land for inheritance. They are named as Caleb son of Jephunneh (Judah), Shemuel son of Ammihud (Simeon), Elidad son of Chislon (Benjamin), Bukki son of Jogli (Dan), Hanniel son of Ephod (Manasseh), Kemuel son of Shiphtan (Ephraim), Elizaphan son of Parnach (Zebulun), Paltiel son of Azzan (Issachar), Ahihud son of Shelomi (Asher), and Pedahel son of Ammihud (Naphtali).

In the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, the LORD commands Moses to have the children of Israel give the Levites forty-eight cities with surrounding pasture lands, taken in proportion to each tribe's inheritance. Six of these are to be cities of refuge, three east of the Jordan and three in Canaan, where a man slayer who kills unintentionally may flee from the avenger of blood until the congregation judges him. The chapter distinguishes murder, committed with iron, stone, or wood weapons or out of hatred and ambush, from killing without hostility or intent. A man slayer must stay in his city of refuge until the high priest dies, and if he leaves, the avenger may kill him without guilt. Murderers must be executed on the testimony of more than one witness, no ransom is allowed, and the land, where the LORD dwells, is polluted by blood that only the blood of the shedder can atone for.

The LORD speaks to Moses in the plains of Moab and commands that the Levites receive cities and that cities of refuge be appointed. He sets out the laws on murder and unintentional killing, and forbids defiling the land because he dwells among the children of Israel.

The children of Israel are commanded to give the Levites cities and pasture lands from their inheritances, with many cities from the larger tribes and few from the smaller. They are also to appoint six cities of refuge, to take no ransom for a murderer, and not to pollute the land.
The Levites are to receive forty-eight cities to dwell in, together with pasture lands for their livestock, possessions, and animals. Six of these cities are the cities of refuge.
The cities given to the Levites total forty-eight with their pasture lands: six cities of refuge plus forty-two others. Each tribe contributes according to the size of its inheritance.

The pasture lands extend one thousand cubits outward from the city wall, measured as two thousand cubits on each of the east, south, west, and north sides, with the city in the middle. They serve the Levites' livestock, possessions, and animals.

Six cities of refuge are to be appointed, three beyond the Jordan and three in Canaan, after Israel crosses the Jordan. They shelter Israelites, strangers, and foreigners who kill unintentionally, protecting them from the avenger until they stand before the congregation for judgment.

The man slayer is one who kills a person unwittingly and may flee to a city of refuge so as not to die before judgment. If the congregation finds him innocent of intent, he lives in the city until the high priest dies, and if he leaves its border and is killed by the avenger, the avenger is not guilty. After the high priest's death he may return to his own land.

The avenger of blood is to put a murderer to death when he meets him. He is not guilty of blood if he kills a man slayer found outside the border of his city of refuge, but the congregation protects the man slayer from him until judgment.

A murderer is one who kills with an iron instrument, a stone, or a wooden weapon, or by shoving out of hatred, lying in wait, or hostile striking. He must surely be put to death by the avenger of blood, on the testimony of witnesses, and no ransom may be taken for his life.

The congregation judges between the striker and the avenger of blood according to the stated ordinances. If the killing was unintentional, it delivers the man slayer from the avenger and restores him to his city of refuge.

Killing is unintentional when a person shoves another suddenly without hostility, hurls something without lying in wait, or casts a stone without seeing him, and was not the victim's enemy or seeking his harm. Such a killer may flee to a city of refuge and receives judgment by the congregation rather than immediate death.

l: murder and blood pollution of the land, Numbers, Chapter 35
s: Blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for blood shed in it except by the blood of the one who shed it. Israel is told not to defile the land it inhabits, because the LORD dwells there among the children of Israel.

The heads of the fathers' households of the family of the children of Gilead, of the tribe of Manasseh, approach Moses and the princes with a concern about the inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters. They argue that if the daughters marry men from other tribes, their land will pass to those tribes and be lost to Manasseh's lot, and it will stay lost even at the jubilee. Moses, speaking according to the LORD's word, affirms that the tribe of Joseph's sons speak rightly and commands that the daughters may marry whom they think best, but only within the family of their father's tribe. The rule is that no inheritance may move from tribe to tribe. The daughters of Zelophehad obey by marrying their father's brothers' sons, so their inheritance stays in the tribe of Manasseh, and the chapter closes by summarizing the commandments given in the plains of Moab.

Moses is approached by the Gilead family heads and the princes regarding the inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters. He commands the children of Israel according to the LORD's word, affirming that the sons of Joseph speak rightly and setting the rule that the daughters must marry within their father's tribe.

The LORD is cited as having commanded that the land be given by lot and that Zelophehad's inheritance go to his daughters. Through Moses, he commands that the daughters may marry whom they think best but only within their father's tribe, so that no inheritance moves from tribe to tribe. The chapter ends by noting these commandments and ordinances were given by Moses in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.

The daughters, named Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah, are the subject of the concern about their inheritance being transferred through marriage. They are commanded to marry within the family of their father's tribe, and they do as the LORD commanded by marrying their father's brothers' sons.

Zelophehad is referred to as the brother of the Gilead family heads, whose inheritance was commanded by the LORD to be given to his daughters. His daughters' marriages keep his inheritance in the tribe of the family of their father.

l: heads of the fathers’ households of the family of the children of Gilead, Numbers, Chapter 36
s: These men, of the family of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, come before Moses and the princes to raise a concern. They argue that the daughters' marriage to men of other tribes would remove the inheritance from their fathers' lot and add it to the other tribe, even at the jubilee. Moses affirms that they speak rightly.

The children of Israel are commanded by Moses, according to the LORD's word, that no inheritance may move from tribe to tribe and that each shall keep the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers. The commandments and ordinances are said to have been given to them in the plains of Moab.

The inheritance, allotted by lot to the tribes, is at risk of transferring between tribes through the marriage of Zelophehad's daughters, and the transfer would be permanent after the jubilee. The ruling establishes that no inheritance shall move from one tribe to another and that each tribe shall keep its own. Zelophehad's inheritance remains in the tribe of Manasseh.

l: marriage of the daughters, Numbers, Chapter 36
s: The daughters are permitted to marry whom they think best, provided the husband is from the family of their father's tribe. Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah marry their father's brothers' sons, within the families of the sons of Manasseh, so their inheritance remains in their father's tribe.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: After Joshua's death, the Israelites ask the LORD who should first fight the Canaanites, and he names Judah. Judah allies with his brother Simeon, defeats the Canaanites and Perizzites at Bezek, captures and mutilates Adoni-Bezek, and takes Jerusalem, Hebron, Debir, and other places. Caleb gives his daughter Achsah to Othniel for capturing Kiriath Sepher, and she also obtains springs of water. The house of Joseph takes Bethel with the help of a man who shows them the entrance, while Benjamin, Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan fail to drive out the inhabitants of their lands. Many Canaanites remain, some put to forced labor, and the Amorites push Dan into the hill country.

l: Judah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: Judah is chosen by the LORD to go up first against the Canaanites and goes with his brother Simeon into each other's lots. He defeats the Canaanites and Perizzites at Bezek, takes Jerusalem, Hebron, Zephath (renamed Hormah), Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, and drives out the hill country inhabitants. He cannot drive out the people of the valley because they had chariots of iron.

l: Simeon, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: Simeon goes up with his brother Judah into Judah's lot after Judah proposes that they fight together and then go into Simeon's lot. He joins Judah in striking the Canaanites of Zephath and utterly destroying it, and the city is named Hormah.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: The LORD answers the Israelites by choosing Judah and declaring that he has delivered the land into Judah's hand. He delivers the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hand and is with Judah and with the house of Joseph. Judah's failure in the valley is attributed to the Canaanites' iron chariots.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: The children of Israel ask the LORD who should go up first against the Canaanites after Joshua's death. When Israel grows strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor rather than utterly driving them out.

l: Canaanites, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: The Canaanites are struck down by Judah at Bezek and in the hill country, the South, and the lowland. Many remain in the land, living among Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali, and some are put to forced labor.

l: Adoni-Bezek, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: Adoni-Bezek is found in Bezek, flees, and is caught, and Judah's forces cut off his thumbs and big toes. He says that seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off scavenged under his table and that God has repaid him. He is brought to Jerusalem and dies there.

l: Caleb, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: Caleb offers his daughter Achsah as wife to whoever takes Kiriath Sepher, and his younger brother Othniel does so. He gives Achsah the upper and lower springs when she asks for a blessing. Hebron is given to him, and he drives out the three sons of Anak.

l: Achsah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: Achsah is given in marriage to Othniel by her father Caleb. When she arrives, she gets Othniel to ask her father for a field, then asks Caleb herself for springs of water because he set her in the land of the South. Caleb gives her the upper and lower springs.

l: Othniel the son of Kenaz, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: Othniel, son of Kenaz and Caleb's younger brother, takes Kiriath Sepher (Debir). As a reward Caleb gives him his daughter Achsah as wife.

l: house of Joseph, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: The house of Joseph goes up against Bethel with the LORD's help and sends spies to scout it. They take the city with the edge of the sword after a man shows them the entrance, sparing the man and his family. Later their hand prevails over the Amorites, who become subject to forced labor.

l: Bethel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: Bethel, formerly named Luz, is spied out and attacked by the house of Joseph. Its watchers' informant shows the entrance, and the city is struck with the edge of the sword.

l: man from Bethel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 1
s: The man is seen by the watchers coming out of the city and shows them the entrance in return for kind treatment. He and his family are let go, and he goes to the land of the Hittites, builds a city, and names it Luz.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: The LORD's angel comes from Gilgal to Bochim and rebukes Israel for disobeying the LORD by making covenants with the land's inhabitants and not breaking down their altars. He announces that the LORD will no longer drive those peoples out, and the people weep and sacrifice at Bochim. Joshua sends the people to their inheritances, and Israel serves the LORD through his lifetime and that of the elders who outlived him; Joshua dies at 110 and is buried in Timnath Heres. A new generation that does not know the LORD then serves Baal and the Ashtaroth, provoking the LORD's anger, so he gives Israel over to raiders and enemies. He raises up judges to save them, but Israel repeatedly relapses after each judge dies, so the LORD declares he will leave the remaining nations to test whether Israel will keep his way.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: The LORD reminds Israel through his angel that he brought them out of Egypt and promised never to break his covenant, but because they disobeyed he says he will not drive out the inhabitants. When the next generation abandons him he delivers Israel to raiders and enemies, then raises up judges and is with each judge, grieved by Israel's groaning. After repeated relapses he declares he will leave the remaining nations to test whether Israel will keep his way.

l: angel of the LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: The LORD's angel goes up from Gilgal to Bochim and speaks the LORD's words to all Israel. He recalls the exodus and the covenant, charges Israel with failing to break down the altars and making covenants with the land's inhabitants, and announces that the LORD will not drive those peoples out. The people weep, and the place is named Bochim.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: Israel weeps and sacrifices at Bochim after the angel's rebuke, then goes out to possess its inheritances and serves the LORD through Joshua's days and those of the elders. Afterward Israel does evil, serves the Baals, Baal and the Ashtaroth, and is handed over to plunderers and enemies. It is distressed, is saved by judges, and keeps relapsing and acting more corruptly than its fathers.

l: Joshua, The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: Joshua, son of Nun and servant of the LORD, sends the people away to their inheritances. Israel serves the LORD all his days and those of the elders who outlived him. He dies at 110 and is buried at Timnath Heres in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash.

l: inhabitants of the land (Canaanite nations), The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: Israel was told to make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land and to break down their altars, but did not obey. As a result the LORD says they will be in Israel's sides and their gods a snare. The LORD says he will no longer drive out the nations Joshua left, and leaves them to test Israel.

l: gods (foreign gods), The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: The inhabitants' gods are foretold as a snare to Israel. The new generation follows and bows down to the gods of surrounding peoples, including Baal and the Ashtaroth, thereby provoking the LORD to anger. Israel's prostitution after other gods continues after each judge dies.

l: new generation (after Joshua's generation), The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: After Joshua's generation is gathered to its fathers, another generation arises that does not know the LORD or the work he did for Israel. It does evil in the LORD's sight, serves the Baals, abandons the LORD, and follows other gods.

l: judges (raised up by the LORD), The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: The LORD raises up judges who save Israel from those who plunder them, and he is with each judge and saves Israel all the days of that judge. Israel does not listen to the judges, and when a judge dies the people turn back and act more corruptly than their fathers.

l: raiders and enemies of Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: The LORD delivers Israel into the hands of raiders who plunder them and sells them to enemies all around, so that Israel can no longer stand before them. The LORD's hand is against Israel wherever they go. The enemies oppress and trouble Israel until the LORD raises up judges to save them.

l: Israel's apostasy and oppression cycle, The Book of Judges, Chapter 2
s: The unit shows a pattern: Israel abandons the LORD for other gods, the LORD's anger burns and he gives them to plunderers, Israel groans, and he raises a judge who saves them. When the judge dies Israel relapses, becoming more corrupt than before. This leads the LORD to leave the remaining nations as a test of whether Israel will keep his way.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 explains that the LORD left certain nations in the land, including the five lords of the Philistines, the Canaanites, the Sidonians and the Hivites, to test Israel and to teach its generations war. Israel lived among these peoples, intermarried with them, and served the Baals and the Asheroth, so the LORD sold them to Cushan Rishathaim king of Mesopotamia for eight years until Othniel the son of Kenaz saved them, after which the land had rest forty years. After Othniel died, Israel again did evil and the LORD strengthened Eglon king of Moab, who oppressed them eighteen years. The Benjamite Ehud, who was left-handed, killed the very fat Eglon with a two-edged sword in his upper room, escaped, and led Israel to strike about ten thousand Moabites at the Jordan fords, giving the land rest for eighty years. Shamgar the son of Anath is then briefly noted for striking six hundred Philistines with an ox goad and saving Israel.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: The LORD left nations in the land to test whether Israel would obey his commandments, and when Israel did evil he sold them into the hand of Cushan Rishathaim. He raised up saviors in response to Israel's cries, Othniel and Ehud, put his Spirit on Othniel, and delivered enemies into their hands. He also strengthened Eglon of Moab against Israel because of Israel's evil.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: Israel lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, intermarried with them, forgot the LORD, and served the Baals and the Asheroth. They served Cushan Rishathaim eight years and Eglon eighteen years, and each time cried to the LORD and was saved. The land had rest forty years after Othniel and eighty years after Moab was subdued.

l: Othniel the son of Kenaz, The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: Othniel, Caleb's younger brother, was raised up by the LORD as a savior after Israel cried out. The LORD's Spirit came on him, he judged Israel and went to war, and his hand prevailed against Cushan Rishathaim. The land had rest forty years, then he died.

l: Cushan Rishathaim king of Mesopotamia, The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: Cushan Rishathaim was the king into whose hand the LORD sold Israel because of their evil, and Israel served him eight years. The LORD delivered him into Othniel's hand, and Othniel's hand prevailed against him.

l: Eglon king of Moab, The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: Eglon was strengthened by the LORD against Israel, gathered the Ammonites and Amalek, struck Israel, and possessed the city of palm trees. Israel served him eighteen years. He was a very fat man, and Ehud killed him with a sword in his cool upper room, where his servants found him dead on the floor.

l: Ehud the son of Gera, The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, was raised up by the LORD as a savior and sent Israel's tribute to Eglon. He made a two-edged sword, hid it on his right thigh, and killed Eglon alone in the upper room under pretense of a message from God, then locked the doors and escaped to Seirah. He blew a trumpet in Ephraim and led Israel to take the Jordan fords and defeat Moab.

l: Shamgar the son of Anath, The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: Shamgar came after Ehud and struck six hundred Philistines with an ox goad. He also saved Israel.

l: Moab, The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: Moab, under its king Eglon, oppressed Israel for eighteen years. After Eglon's death, Israelites led by Ehud took the Jordan fords, struck about ten thousand Moabite strong men and men of valor, and let none escape. Moab was subdued that day under Israel's hand.

l: sword (Ehud's sword), The Book of Judges, Chapter 3
s: Ehud made the sword himself with two edges and a cubit in length, and wore it under his clothing on his right thigh. He drew it with his left hand and thrust it into Eglon so that the handle went in after the blade and the fat closed over it. He did not draw it out, and it came out behind.

l: The Book of Judges, The Book of Judges, Chapter 4
s: After Ehud's death, the children of Israel again did evil, and the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, whose army captain Sisera commanded nine hundred iron chariots and oppressed Israel for twenty years. Deborah, a prophetess and judge, summoned Barak and relayed the LORD's command to lead ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun to Mount Tabor; Barak agreed only if she went with him, and she told him the honor would go to a woman. Sisera gathered his chariots and army at the river Kishon, where the LORD confused them before Barak and all of Sisera's army fell by the sword. Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, who covered him, gave him milk, and killed him in his sleep by driving a tent peg through his temples. Barak arrived to find Sisera dead, and the children of Israel increasingly prevailed until they destroyed Jabin.

l: Deborah, The Book of Judges, Chapter 4
s: Deborah, a prophetess and wife of Lappidoth, judged Israel from under her palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, and the children of Israel came to her for judgment. She called Barak, relayed the LORD's command to attack Sisera, agreed to go with him, and told him the honor would go to a woman. She later told Barak to go because the LORD had delivered Sisera into his hand.

l: Barak the son of Abinoam, The Book of Judges, Chapter 4
s: Barak son of Abinoam of Kedesh Naphtali was summoned by Deborah and told to lead ten thousand men to Mount Tabor. He would go only if she went with him, gathered Zebulun and Naphtali, and went down from Tabor to pursue Sisera's army to Harosheth of the Gentiles. When he reached Jael's tent, he found Sisera already dead.

l: Sisera, The Book of Judges, Chapter 4
s: Sisera, captain of Jabin's army, lived in Harosheth of the Gentiles and gathered his nine hundred iron chariots and his people to the river Kishon after hearing Barak had gone to Mount Tabor. His army was routed, and he abandoned his chariot and fled on foot to Jael's tent. There he asked for water, was given milk, asked Jael to deny his presence, and was killed in his sleep with a tent peg through his temples.

l: Jael, The Book of Judges, Chapter 4
s: Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, welcomed the fleeing Sisera into her tent, covered him with a rug, and gave him milk. While he slept deeply, she struck a tent peg through his temples into the ground with a hammer, killing him. She then showed his body to Barak when he came pursuing.

l: Jabin, The Book of Judges, Chapter 4
s: Jabin, king of Canaan, reigned in Hazor, and the LORD sold Israel into his hand, with Sisera as his army's captain. He had peace with the house of Heber the Kenite. God subdued him before Israel, and Israel prevailed more and more until they destroyed him.

l: LORD, The Book of Judges, Chapter 4
s: The LORD sold Israel into Jabin's hand because of their evil, and commanded through Deborah that Barak lead the attack on Sisera, promising to draw Sisera to the river Kishon and deliver him. He confused Sisera, his chariots, and his army before Barak. God subdued Jabin before Israel that day.

l: Israel, The Book of Judges, Chapter 4
